analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling along the Atlantic coast and near Florida.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Energy Committee without a vote since its April 2025 introduction, with 17 Democratic and independent senators behind it and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to make it illegal for the federal government to sell or authorize offshore oil and gas leases in four areas: the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas [S2]. This would permanently protect the East Coast and waters around Florida from offshore drilling, which supporters say shields coastal tourism, fishing, and shoreline communities from the risk of oil spills [S1]. The ban would apply to future exploration, development, and production of oil, gas, or any other minerals in those waters [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities along the Atlantic seaboard and around Florida, especially people whose livelihoods depend on tourism, commercial fishing, and clean beaches. Beach towns from Maine to Florida depend on unpolluted shorelines; a single offshore spill can shut down fisheries and tourism for years. Residents also avoid the industrialization of their coastline from drilling platforms and support infrastructure.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Secretary of the Interior from issuing any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production of oil, natural gas, or other minerals in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas [S2].
The ban is written to override any other provision of law, making it permanent rather than something a future administration could reverse through the routine five-year leasing process [S2].
The covered planning areas span the entire Atlantic coast and the waters around Florida, protecting the shoreline economies of coastal states from New England to South Florida [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies lose access to potential new drilling territory in the Atlantic. Broader energy consumers could theoretically face marginally reduced future domestic supply, though these areas currently have little or no active production, so the near-term effect on fuel prices is small. The federal government forgoes potential lease revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently forecloses access to potentially significant domestic oil and gas reserves in the Atlantic, which opponents argue limits future energy supply at a time of concern about prices and energy security [S2].

A statutory ban removes the flexibility of the regular planning process, where each administration weighs drilling against environmental and economic factors in five-year programs; this bill takes that decision away from future administrations regardless of conditions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the coastal states covered, the protection is concrete and the cost is largely hypothetical: the Atlantic planning areas have little active drilling today, so the bill mostly locks out future risk rather than shutting down existing production. The tradeoff is real for national energy policy, since the reserves become permanently off-limits, but for the people who live and work on that coastline the bill trades uncertain future oil supply for protection of industries that employ them now.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2025 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it has stayed without a hearing or vote [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker and 16 cosponsors introduced the bill on April 10, 2025 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day; no further action appears in the record [S4].
All 16 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost, since nothing has happened beyond introduction. If the bill dies in committee, offshore drilling companies keep their future access to Atlantic waters, and coastal communities remain dependent on whichever administration is in power to keep drilling away from their shores.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill is stalled

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the COAST Anti-Drilling Act and recruited 16 cosponsors.

for.name: 16 Senate cosponsors
for.role: All Democrats and independents (14 D, 2 I), including Sens. Whitehouse, Markey, Warren, Sanders, and King
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; none from the Republican conference.

against.name: Mike Lee
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill since it was referred to his committee on April 10, 2025.

against.name: Offshore drilling industry
against.role: Oil and gas producers seeking Atlantic leasing
against.what_they_did: Industry groups have long opposed Atlantic drilling bans, arguing the areas hold valuable energy resources.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors are Democrats or independents and no Republican has signed on; the bill sits with a Republican-controlled Senate committee that has not acted on it [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill permanently removes four Atlantic planning areas from leasing, ending these companies' potential future access to East Coast waters. Industry interest runs against the coastal communities that would bear the spill risk from their operations.
Beach economies from New England to Florida depend on clean water and shorelines; the ban protects them from the risk of drilling accidents and spills.
Fishing grounds in the covered planning areas would be protected from drilling activity and potential contamination.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and the bill referred to a committee controlled by the opposing party, it is very unlikely to advance in this Congress. The most likely outcome is that it sits in the Energy and Natural Resources Committee until the session ends, as similar coastal drilling bans have done in past Congresses.
